questions.question: What are character streams in Java and what are their main classes?
questions.title: Java Character Streams Overview
questions.direct_answer: Character streams read and write Unicode characters using Reader and Writer as abstract base classes. Key classes include FileReader and FileWriter for file text I/O, BufferedReader and BufferedWriter for buffered text, StringReader and StringWriter for in-memory text, and PrintWriter for formatted output.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of character stream classes and their appropriate use cases in text file operations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using FileReader without specifying encoding which uses platform default encoding and causes cross-platform bugs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate that new FileReader(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) is the correct way since Java 11 to avoid encoding issues

sections.title: Character Streams Handle Text, One Character at a Time
sections.content:
A **character stream** reads and writes text one character at a time. The two base classes are `Reader` for input and `Writer` for output.

Why they exist: a file on disk is just bytes, but text isn't the same as bytes. A character stream sits on top of the bytes and turns them into real characters, so you never hand-decode anything.

How it works under the hood: every character stream carries a **charset**, the table that maps bytes to characters. Java keeps text as UTF-16 in memory, and the stream converts to or from the file's encoding — usually UTF-8 — on the way in and out.

The classes fall into a few simple groups:
- `FileReader` and `FileWriter` read and write files as text.
- `BufferedReader` and `BufferedWriter` add a buffer and the handy `readLine` method.
- `StringReader` and `StringWriter` work on text held in memory.
- `PrintWriter` adds `printf`-style formatting.

A non-obvious detail trips up most freshers: an old `FileReader` with no charset picks the platform default, so the same file reads fine on a laptop and breaks on the server.

> **The gotcha:** always pass a charset like `StandardCharsets.UTF_8` — never trust the platform default.

sections.title: How Bytes Become Characters
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR F["Bytes on disk
UTF-8"] --> R["InputStreamReader
decodes with a charset"] R --> B["BufferedReader
adds readLine"] B --> A["Your app
UTF-16 chars"] ``` The reader decodes bytes into characters; the buffer batches them so the disk isn't hit once per character.

sections.title: Character Streams at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Character streams|~16-bit chars, text|Reader / Writer|charset decoding|handles Unicode
blue|Core classes|~FileReader / FileWriter|BufferedReader / BufferedWriter|InputStreamReader bridge|PrintWriter
emerald|Use|~any text data|specify the charset (UTF-8)|readLine() per line|don't use byte streams for text

sections.title: Reading Configuration with Character Streams
When Character Streams Are Essential
sections.content:
Use character streams when working with **text data meant for humans**: reading application.properties or YAML configs where encoding matters across different servers, writing log files where you need line-by-line text output, processing CSV files with text columns, generating HTML or JSON responses in web applications.

Choose **BufferedReader** over plain FileReader for any file larger than a few KB to avoid thousands of small disk reads.

Use **FileReader with explicit charset** since Java 11 to prevent encoding bugs when your Linux server (UTF-8 default) processes a config file created on Windows (often Cp1252 default).

Avoid character streams for binary data like images or PDFs — byte streams are faster and prevent corruption.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **FileReader without charset**: Calling new FileReader(file) uses the platform default encoding which differs between Windows and Linux, causing mysterious character corruption bugs when deployed. Always use new FileReader(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) in Java 11+.
- **Forgetting BufferedReader**: Wrapping FileReader directly without BufferedReader causes one disk read per character which is 1000x slower for typical config files.
- **Not closing streams**: Forgetting try-with-resources leaves file handles open until garbage collection, eventually hitting OS limits and causing "Too many open files" errors in production.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Reader and Writer**: abstract base classes for all character stream operations, handle Unicode conversion automatically
- **FileReader/FileWriter**: read from and write to files as character data, always specify charset in Java 11+ to avoid platform encoding issues
- **BufferedReader/BufferedWriter**: wrap other readers/writers to add buffering, dramatically improving performance by reducing system calls
- **StringReader/StringWriter**: in-memory character streams useful for testing and string manipulation without disk I/O
- **PrintWriter**: adds printf-style formatting methods and silently suppresses IOExceptions, check errors via checkError()
- **Character vs Byte Streams**: use character streams for text (configs, logs, CSV), byte streams for binary data (images, serialized objects)
- **try-with-resources**: always use this construct to guarantee stream closure even when exceptions occur, preventing resource leaks

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Character streams are Java's way of reading and writing text data as Unicode characters. The two base classes are Reader for input and Writer for output. For files, you'd use FileReader and FileWriter. The key thing is that character streams handle encoding automatically — they convert between Java's internal UTF-16 and whatever encoding you specify, usually UTF-8. BufferedReader and BufferedWriter wrap other streams to add buffering, which makes file operations way faster because you're not hitting the disk for every single character. Then there's StringReader and StringWriter for working with text in memory without touching the file system — these are super useful in unit tests. PrintWriter is special because it adds convenience methods like println and printf for formatted output, but it also suppresses exceptions so you need to call checkError to see if something went wrong. One major pitfall freshers hit is using new FileReader without specifying the charset. That uses the platform default encoding, so your app works fine on your Windows laptop but breaks on the Linux server because the encodings don't match. Since Java 11, you should always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8 as the second argument. For reading config files or logs, you'd typically use BufferedReader wrapping FileReader with UTF-8 encoding, and always put it in a try-with-resources block so it gets closed automatically.

questions.question: How do you read a text file line by line in Java?
questions.title: Reading Text Files Line by Line
questions.direct_answer: Use BufferedReader.readLine() in a loop, checking for null to detect end of stream. Modern Java offers BufferedReader.lines() which returns a Stream of strings. For simple cases, Files.lines(Path) is a one-liner. Always use try-with-resources for automatic stream closure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to write correct file reading code with proper resource management
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not checking for null on readLine() leading to incomplete reads, or forgetting to close the stream causing resource leaks
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate Files.lines() and explain lazy loading versus eager loading trade-offs for large files

sections.title: Three Ways to Read a File Line by Line
sections.content:
Reading a file **line by line** means pulling one line of text at a time until the file ends. It's one of the most common things a backend app does.

The oldest way uses a `BufferedReader` and its `readLine` method in a loop. `readLine` returns the next line, or `null` when there's nothing left, so the loop stops on `null`.

Java 8 added a streaming option, `BufferedReader.lines()`, which gives a `Stream<String>`. Java 11 made it a one-liner with `Files.lines(path)`. These read **lazily** — one line enters memory at a time — so even a huge log file won't blow the heap.

The three choices line up like this:
- A `readLine` loop when each line needs custom logic or a counter.
- `Files.lines` for quick filtering or mapping.
- `Files.readAllLines` only for small files, since it loads everything at once.

Every one of them needs `try-with-resources` so the file handle closes cleanly.

> **The gotcha:** `readLine` signals end of file with `null`, not `-1` — forget that check and the loop spins forever.

sections.title: The Classic readLine Loop
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["Open BufferedReader
in try-with-resources"] --> B["line = readLine()"] B --> C{"line is null?"} C -- No --> D["Process the line"] D --> B C -- Yes --> E["End of file
close the reader"] ``` The loop keeps reading until readLine returns null, which is the only end-of-file signal.

sections.title: Reading Text Line by Line
sections.content:
amber|Classic|~BufferedReader(new FileReader(f))|while ((line = readLine()) != null)|in try-with-resources|null = EOF
blue|Charset-safe|~InputStreamReader(in, UTF_8)|wrap in BufferedReader|avoids the platform default|recommended
emerald|Modern|~Files.readAllLines(path)|Files.lines(path) stream|less boilerplate|the stream is lazy + closeable

sections.title: Line Reading Approaches Compared
sections.content:
| Approach | Code Complexity | Memory Usage | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|
| BufferedReader.readLine() loop | Medium - explicit null check | Low - one line at a time | Complex parsing with state |
| BufferedReader.lines() stream | Low - functional style | Low - lazy evaluation | Filter and transform operations |
| Files.lines(Path) | Lowest - one liner | Low - lazy evaluation | Simple read entire file |
| Files.readAllLines(Path) | Lowest - one liner | High - loads entire file | Small files needing multiple passes |

sections.title: Reading Application Logs Line by Line
Choosing the Right Approach
sections.content:
Use **Files.lines(Path)** for simple filtering, mapping, or collecting lines when you don't need line numbers or complex state. It's the cleanest one-liner for most cases.

Use **BufferedReader.readLine() loop** when you need to track line numbers, maintain state across lines (like parsing multi-line records), or handle errors mid-stream without terminating the entire operation.

Use **BufferedReader.lines()** when you already have a BufferedReader from another source like a network socket or compressed stream.

Avoid **Files.readAllLines()** for large files — it loads the entire file into memory at once, which can cause OutOfMemoryError on multi-gigabyte log files. For configuration files under 1MB, readAllLines() is fine and convenient for multiple passes over the data.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not checking for null**: The loop while(line = reader.readLine()) without the != null check never terminates or causes NullPointerException on the last iteration.
- **Forgetting to close Stream**: Calling Files.lines() without try-with-resources leaves the file handle open, eventually hitting OS file descriptor limits.
- **Using readLine() inside stream operations**: Mixing while loops with .lines() streams causes confusing bugs because readLine() consumes lines the stream also tries to read.
- **No charset specification**: Calling Files.lines(path) without a charset uses the platform default, causing encoding bugs across environments.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **BufferedReader.readLine()**: returns null at end of stream, not empty string — always check for null in while condition
- **Files.lines(Path)**: returns a Stream that must be closed with try-with-resources, lazily reads one line at a time
- **Lazy evaluation**: Stream-based approaches don't load the entire file into memory, safe for multi-gigabyte log files
- **try-with-resources**: essential for all file reading to guarantee closure even when exceptions occur mid-read
- **Charset specification**: always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8 explicitly to avoid platform-dependent encoding bugs
- **Line terminators**: readLine() strips \n and \r\n automatically, you don't get them in the returned string
- **Performance**: BufferedReader with 8KB default buffer is fast enough for most cases, no need for larger buffers

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: There are three main ways to read a file line by line in Java. The traditional way is using BufferedReader with readLine in a while loop. You'd create a BufferedReader, then loop while readLine returns non-null, because null means you've hit the end of the file. The key thing is always checking for null in your loop condition. The second way is using BufferedReader.lines which returns a Stream of strings. This lets you use functional-style operations like filter and map. The cleanest approach for simple cases is Files.lines which takes a Path and gives you a Stream in one line. All three approaches are lazy — they read one line at a time, not the whole file into memory, so they work fine on multi-gigabyte log files. The critical thing freshers miss is resource management. You must use try-with-resources for all three approaches. With Files.lines, if you forget the try block, the file handle stays open and you'll eventually hit the OS limit on open files. Another common mistake is not checking for null when using readLine in a loop — your code will either hang forever or throw a NullPointerException. For deciding which to use, I'd pick Files.lines for simple filtering or transformation, the traditional readLine loop when I need to track line numbers or maintain state across lines, and avoid readAllLines unless the file is tiny because that loads everything into memory at once.

questions.question: How do you write text to a file in Java?
questions.title: Writing Text Files in Java
questions.direct_answer: Use Files.writeString() for simple string writes, Files.write() for lists of lines, or BufferedWriter wrapping FileWriter for more control. Use StandardOpenOption.APPEND to append instead of overwrite. Always specify charset explicitly and use try-with-resources for resource management.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical file writing knowledge with modern Java APIs and understanding of append versus overwrite modes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing how to append to a file versus overwrite it, or forgetting to flush or close the stream leading to data loss
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate Files.writeString() and Files.write() as cleaner alternatives to verbose stream boilerplate code

sections.title: Writing Text: One-Liners and the Append Trap
sections.content:
Writing text to a file means sending characters out to disk as a file's contents. Modern Java makes the common cases tiny.

For a single `String`, `Files.writeString(path, text)` does it in **one line**. For a list of lines, `Files.write(path, lines)` writes each element on its own line. Both open, write, and close the file for you.

When the writing happens in a loop, a `BufferedWriter` is the better fit. It stays open across many writes and batches them, so the disk isn't hit on every call.

The behavior most freshers miss is **overwrite versus append**:
- By default every write replaces the file's contents.
- Passing `StandardOpenOption.APPEND` adds to the end instead.

A buffered writer also holds text in memory until it's flushed, so an unclosed writer can silently lose the last lines.

> **The gotcha:** logging in a loop without `APPEND` overwrites each time — you end up with one line, not thousands.

sections.title: Picking a Writer and a Mode
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["Need to write text"] --> B{"How much
at once?"} B -- One string --> C["Files.writeString"] B -- A list of lines --> D["Files.write"] B -- Many writes in a loop --> E["BufferedWriter"] C --> F{"Append?"} D --> F E --> F F -- Yes --> G["Add the APPEND option"] F -- No --> H["Default overwrites"] ``` The shape of the data picks the method; the APPEND option decides overwrite versus add-to-end.

sections.title: Writing Text to a File
sections.content:
amber|Open|~BufferedWriter(new FileWriter(f))|FileWriter(f, true) to append|try-with-resources|UTF-8 via OutputStreamWriter
blue|Write|~write(String)|newLine() for line breaks|PrintWriter for printf / println|format as needed
emerald|Commit|~close() flushes|or call flush()|missing close = lost text|Files.writeString is simplest

sections.title: Step 1: Choose Based on Data Structure
sections.content: Start by identifying what you're writing. If you have a **single String** (like a JSON response or serialized object), Files.writeString(path, content, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) is the simplest choice. If you have a **List or Collection of strings** where each element should become a line (like CSV rows or log entries), Files.write(path, lines, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) handles newline insertion automatically. If you're writing **incrementally in a loop** or from a stream source (like processing records from a database cursor), use BufferedWriter to avoid opening and closing the file repeatedly. For **formatted output** with printf-style patterns, wrap BufferedWriter with PrintWriter for access to format() and printf() methods.

sections.title: Step 2: Decide Append or Overwrite
sections.content: By default, all write methods **overwrite** the file if it exists. To append to an existing file, pass **StandardOpenOption.APPEND** as an additional parameter. For Files.writeString(), use Files.writeString(path, content, StandardCharsets.UTF_8, StandardOpenOption.CREATE, StandardOpenOption.APPEND). For BufferedWriter, use Files.newBufferedWriter(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8, StandardOpenOption.APPEND). The CREATE option ensures the file is created if it doesn't exist. For log files that grow over time, always use APPEND mode. For configuration files or reports that should be regenerated fresh each time, use the default overwrite behavior. Forgetting APPEND when writing logs leads to only the last log entry being saved, a frustrating bug for freshers to debug.

sections.title: Writing Application Logs with Different Approaches
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting APPEND mode**: Using Files.writeString() in a loop without StandardOpenOption.APPEND causes each call to overwrite the file, leaving only the last write. Logs end up with one entry instead of thousands.
- **Not flushing BufferedWriter**: Buffered writes stay in memory until the buffer fills or close() is called. If the app crashes before closing, recent writes are lost. Always use try-with-resources which flushes and closes automatically.
- **Manual newline handling**: Writing content + \n instead of using writer.newLine() causes Windows/Linux newline mismatches. Use newLine() for platform-independent line separators.
- **No charset specification**: Omitting charset uses platform default, causing encoding bugs when deployed to servers with different locales.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Files.writeString()**: Java 11+ one-liner for writing a single string, handles resource management internally
- **Files.write()**: writes a List of strings as lines, automatically inserting line separators between elements
- **StandardOpenOption.APPEND**: adds content to existing file instead of overwriting, essential for log files
- **BufferedWriter**: best for incremental writes in loops or streams, reduces disk I/O by batching writes
- **Charset specification**: always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8 explicitly to avoid platform-dependent encoding bugs
- **writer.newLine()**: use instead of \n for platform-independent line separators that work on Windows and Unix
- **Flushing**: BufferedWriter buffers in memory, must flush or close to guarantee data reaches disk

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: For writing text to files, Java 11 introduced really clean APIs that make it much simpler than the old way. If you're writing a single string, Files.writeString is a one-liner — just pass the path, your content, and StandardCharsets.UTF_8 for the encoding. If you have a list of strings and want each to be a line, use Files.write which handles the newline insertion automatically. Both of these manage resources internally so you don't need try-with-resources. The traditional approach is BufferedWriter wrapping FileWriter, which gives you more control and is better when you're writing incrementally in a loop because it keeps the file open and buffers writes. By default, all these methods overwrite the file. To append instead — like when writing to a log file — you pass StandardOpenOption.APPEND as an extra parameter. For example, Files.writeString takes CREATE and APPEND options after the charset. One mistake freshers make is forgetting the APPEND option when logging in a loop. Each write overwrites the file, so you end up with only the last log entry instead of all of them. Another pitfall is not closing or flushing BufferedWriter. Writes are buffered in memory, so if your app crashes before closing, you lose the recent writes. That's why try-with-resources is critical — it automatically flushes and closes even if exceptions occur. For charset, always specify UTF-8 explicitly. The default changes based on the OS, so your file might be readable on your Windows laptop but garbled on the Linux server.

questions.question: What is PrintWriter and when do you use it?
questions.title: PrintWriter in Java
questions.direct_answer: PrintWriter is a Writer that adds convenience methods like print(), println(), printf(), and format() for formatted text output. It never throws IOException directly — errors are tracked internally and accessed via checkError(). Use it for formatted reports, HTTP response bodies in servlets, and any scenario where you need printf-style formatting.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of PrintWriter's unique error handling model and its practical use cases in web applications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing PrintWriter suppresses IOExceptions silently — errors go unnoticed unless you explicitly call checkError()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that servlet response.getWriter() returns a PrintWriter and explain why silent error handling makes sense in that context

sections.title: PrintWriter: Formatted Output That Hides Its Errors
sections.content:
A **`PrintWriter`** is a writer with convenient print methods. It gives you `print`, `println`, `printf`, and `format`, the same calls as `System.out`.

Why it exists: plain writers only push raw characters. `PrintWriter` adds formatting and line handling, so building a report or an HTTP response reads naturally.

How it behaves differently: a `PrintWriter` never throws an `IOException` from a write. It records the error internally instead, and `checkError` reports it later.

That design is deliberate for servlets — `HttpServletResponse.getWriter` returns a `PrintWriter`, because a half-sent response shouldn't blow up mid-render.

A few traits worth knowing:
- It wraps any `Writer` or `OutputStream`.
- It can auto-flush on `println` when constructed with that flag.
- It converts everything to text, so it's useless for binary data.

> **The gotcha:** because errors stay hidden, a disk-full failure passes unnoticed unless `checkError` is called.

sections.title: Where the Error Goes
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["println / printf call"] --> B["Format the text"] B --> C{"Write fails?"} C -- No --> D["Text goes out"] C -- Yes --> E["Set internal error flag
no exception thrown"] E --> F["checkError reveals it later"] ``` A write never throws; the error hides behind a flag until checkError is asked.

sections.title: PrintWriter at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|PrintWriter|~text output: print / println|printf / format support|never throws on write|check checkError()
blue|Wraps|~a Writer or OutputStream|a File or path directly|an autoFlush option|a charset argument
emerald|Use|~formatted text / logs|console-like output|System.out is a cousin (PrintStream)|close to flush

sections.title: Using PrintWriter for Report Generation
When PrintWriter Shines
sections.content:
Use **PrintWriter** when you need **printf-style formatting** with %s, %d, %.2f specifiers for aligned columnar output in reports or tables. It's essential in **servlet response writing** where HttpServletResponse.getWriter() returns a PrintWriter for generating HTML, JSON, or plain text responses.

Choose it for **logging to files** when you want convenience methods like println() instead of manually appending newlines. PrintWriter works well for **formatted console output** in command-line tools where you need table-like alignment.

Avoid it when you need **immediate IOException feedback** — if disk full or network errors must be handled immediately, use BufferedWriter which throws exceptions directly. Also avoid for **binary data** — PrintWriter is text-only and converts all data to characters.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Ignoring checkError()**: PrintWriter suppresses IOExceptions completely, so errors like disk full or permission denied go unnoticed unless you explicitly call checkError() after writing. Critical data loss can occur silently.
- **Assuming auto-flush**: By default, PrintWriter only auto-flushes on println() if constructed with autoFlush=true for streams. File-backed PrintWriters don't auto-flush at all — data stays buffered until close().
- **Mixing print and write**: Using print() and write() methods together causes confusion because print() converts objects to strings while write() expects raw characters, leading to formatting inconsistencies.
- **Platform newlines**: println() uses the platform's line separator, which differs between Windows (\r\n) and Linux (\n), potentially breaking parsers expecting consistent line endings.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Silent error handling**: PrintWriter never throws IOException from print/println/printf methods, errors are internal
- **checkError()**: must call this method explicitly to detect if any write operations failed during the stream's lifetime
- **printf and format**: support C-style format strings like %s, %d, %.2f for formatted output with alignment and precision
- **Auto-flush**: only occurs on println() when PrintWriter is constructed with autoFlush=true parameter for stream output
- **Servlet integration**: HttpServletResponse.getWriter() returns PrintWriter because HTTP response writing shouldn't throw exceptions
- **Platform line separator**: println() uses System.lineSeparator() which differs across operating systems
- **No charset in constructor**: must wrap an existing Writer (like OutputStreamWriter) to specify charset, or use Files.newBufferedWriter()

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: PrintWriter is a character stream class that adds convenience methods for formatted output. It gives you print, println, printf, and format methods, basically making file writing as easy as System.out.println. The unique thing about PrintWriter is its error handling — it never throws IOException directly. Instead, errors are recorded internally and you check for them by calling checkError. This makes it really convenient for scenarios where you don't want exception handling to clutter your code, like generating reports or writing HTTP responses. In fact, when you call response.getWriter in a servlet, you get a PrintWriter back because you don't want the response to crash mid-write if there's a network hiccup. The main use cases are formatted reports where you need printf-style formatting with percent-s and percent-d specifiers for aligned columns, writing servlet responses, and general text file output when you want the convenience of println instead of manually adding newlines. One critical mistake freshers make is not calling checkError after writing. Since PrintWriter swallows exceptions, you could have a disk full error and never know unless you explicitly check. Your app thinks it wrote the data successfully but the file is incomplete or empty. Another thing is auto-flush — by default, PrintWriter doesn't auto-flush on every write. Data stays buffered until you close the stream or the buffer fills up. If you need immediate writes, you can enable auto-flush in the constructor, but it only works for println, not print. For choosing between PrintWriter and BufferedWriter, use PrintWriter when you need formatting or convenience methods, but use BufferedWriter when you need immediate exception feedback or don't want silent error suppression.

speakable_v2.hook: PrintWriter makes file writing feel like System.out, with print and printf. The catch: it swallows write errors instead of throwing them.

beats.text: A `PrintWriter` wraps a writer and adds friendly print methods. It brings print, println, printf, and format, the very calls people know from System.out, and it formats values into text automatically.
Plain writers only push raw characters. PrintWriter layers formatting and line handling on top, which makes reports and HTTP responses far easier to build.

items: It wraps any writer or output stream as the real target.
It can auto-flush on println when that flag's switched on.
It only deals in text, so binary data stays off-limits.

beats.text: In a servlet, response.getWriter hands back a PrintWriter, and that's no accident. The reply streams out as HTML or JSON. A mid-render hiccup won't throw and corrupt the half-sent response.

items: Errors stay hidden, so a disk-full failure slips by unless checkError gets called.
Auto-flush sits off by default, a non-obvious reason text can linger unwritten until close.

speakable_v2.cap: So PrintWriter trades loud exceptions for convenience. Lean on it for formatted text, but call checkError when the write really matters.
